title: Cap. VII §6: Breve compendium — causes yes, modes and merit-respect no
pass_a_gloss: Placeus calls the prior arguments especially weak for immediate imputation; Garissoles praises them and compresses: causes, effects, and modes compared — Christ and Adam share the same merit-respect and meritorious efficiency. Placeus grants comparing causes and effects, denies same modes and same respect: nature vs grace, carnal generation vs free gift, propagating inhering sin vs remitting it, one reatus vs all. Christ's merit is debt-payment, surety satisfaction, made sin for us, received by faith — nothing like said of Adam. Propagated damning vice from Adam does not imply propagated justifying righteousness from Christ; opponents' arguments would as easily prove that. Hold likeness of merit if you will, but a large unlikeness in how merit is communicated.
pass_b_english: What is weaker than the foregoing arguments for the imputation of Adam's sin, especially the immediate? Yet their author praises them, and, that they may be repeated without the reader's disgust, reduces them into a short compendium. Causes are compared, he says; the effects of the causes are compared; the modes of the effects are compared. The causes, namely Christ and Adam, are compared because each has the same respect and relation to those effects which they produce in men — namely the respect of merit; because each produces not only by any efficiency whatever, or however named, but by meritorious efficiency — the one justification, the other condemnation. That causes and the effects of causes are compared I confess; I deny the modes of the effects. I deny that each cause has the same respect to those effects which they produce in men: for they have rather a diverse. For the one produces its effect by nature, the other by grace; that by carnal generation, this by free gift; that by propagating into us inhering sin which merits condemnation, this by remitting to us that inhering sin; that has a relation to only one sin and guilt, this to all the guilts of all our sins. How then will it be demonstrated that the respect of each is the same, and that of merit? Christ merited for us remission of sins. For he paid our debts. He satisfied Divine Justice in our place. He suffered the death which we had deserved, and, as the Apostle speaks, was made sin for us, that we might be the righteousness of God in him. He freely gave us his own merit: we receive it offered through faith. This was the Father's mind, this the Son's, this the will, this the counsel, this the aim. Scripture everywhere inculcates it. Does it say such a thing of Adam? Did he want by that disobedience of his to merit death for us? Did he sin in our place? Did he give us that merit of his? Do we receive it through some act of our mind or will? How then is each said to have the same respect, the same relation? Or if an inhering vice sufficient for our being damned was propagated into us from Adam, does it follow that an inhering righteousness sufficient for our being justified was propagated into us from Christ? Yet let those who oppose us in this cause see, I ask, whether this cannot be gathered from D. Garissoles's Arguments equally with the antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. Therefore however great a likeness of merit — not now identity — be said to be between each cause, it must be tightly held that in the mode of communicating merit no small unlikeness ought to be observed.
source_text: Quid superioribus argumentis pro imputatione peccati Adae, praesertim immediata, debilius? Laudat tamen ea suus auctor, et, ut sine Lectoris fastidio repeti possint, in breve compendium redigit. Comparantur, inquit, causae, comparantur causarum effecta, comparantur effectorum modi. Causae, scilicet Christus et Adamus, comparantur, quod utraque eundem respectum et σχέσιν habeat ad illa, quae in hominibus producunt, effecta, nempe respectum meriti; quod utraque non tantum per quamcunque efficientiam, aut quomodolibet dictam, sed per meritoriam efficientiam producant, altera iustificationem, altera condemnationem. Causas et causarum effecta comparari fateor; nego effectorum modos. Nego utramque causam eundem respectum habere ad illa, quae in hominibus producunt, effecta: habent enim diversum potius. Altera enim per naturam, altera per gratiam producit effectum suum; Illa per generationem carnalem, haec per gratuitam donationem; Illa propagando in nos peccatum inhaerens quod meretur condemnationem, haec remittendo nobis illud peccatum inhaerens; Illa σχέσιν habet ad unum tantum peccatum et reatum, haec ad omnes reatus omnium peccatorum nostrorum. Quomodo ergo demonstrabitur, eundem esse utriusque respectum, et quidem meriti? Meruit nobis Christus remissionem peccatorum. Is enim debita nostra exsolvit. Is Iustitiae Divinae loco nostro satisfecit. Is mortem, quam eramus commeriti, passus est, et, ut loquitur Apostolus, factus est pro nobis peccatum, ut essemus iustitia Dei in ipso. Is suum nobis ultro meritum dedit: nos id per fidem oblatum accipimus. Haec Patris, haec Filii mens, haec voluntas, hoc consilium, hic scopus fuit. Id Scriptura passim inculcat. Dicit-ne de Adamo tale quid? Voluit-ne is nobis sua illa inobedientia mortem mereri? Peccavit-ne loco nostro? Dedit-ne nobis suum illud meritum? Illud-ne accipimus per aliquem mentis voluntatisve actum nostrum? Quomodo ergo dicitur utriusque idem esse respectus, eadem σχέσις? An si vitium inhaerens nobis damnandis sufficiens in nos ab Adamo propagatum est, consequens est, iustitiam inhaerentem nobis iustificandis sufficientem in nos a Christo propagatam fuisse? Videant tamen, quaeso, qui nobis in hac causa adversantur, annon hoc aeque ac imputatio antecedens Adamici peccati Argumentis D. Garissolii colligi possit? Quantacunque igitur inter utramque causam, non iam identitas, sed similitudo meriti dicatur esse; arcte tenendum est, in modo communicandi meriti haud exiguam dissimilitudinem observari debere.

choices.decision: Keep Garissoles summary with Placeus mode/merit reply together
